books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage written for this question; facts from the grounding books.
stimulus.text: The Fugitive Slave Act was enforced in the North, and the North answered back. In February 1851 a crowd in Boston pulled Shadrach Minkins, a waiter seized as a runaway, out of a courtroom and sent him on to Canada. That September, near Christiana, Pennsylvania, Black residents and their neighbors fought off a Maryland slaveholder's party, and the slaveholder was killed. A month later, in Syracuse, New York, a crowd freed William “Jerry” Henry from the officers holding him. And in June 1854 federal troops marched Anthony Burns, a waiter seized in Boston, through the streets to a ship bound for Virginia.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The four episodes in the passage share which pattern?

options.text: Federal courts freed every accused runaway they heard.
options.misconception: Only Burns reached a federal hearing's end, and he was returned; the others were freed by crowds before any court freed them.

options.text: Northern crowds resisted by force, but federal power sometimes prevailed.
Southern slaveholders accepted the rescues without a fight.
options.misconception: The slaveholder at Christiana was killed in the fight, and Burns's claimant pressed his case to rendition — no acceptance.

options.text: State governments repealed the Fugitive Slave Act in response.
options.misconception: Background from the books: no state repealed the federal act — states could not repeal federal law; some passed personal liberty laws to hinder it instead.

rationales.A: Only Burns reached a federal hearing's end, and he was returned; the others were freed by crowds before any court freed them.
rationales.B: Minkins, Christiana, and Jerry were all freed by crowds or neighbors, while Burns was marched to a ship by federal troops — resistance and rendition side by side.
rationales.C: The slaveholder at Christiana was killed in the fight, and Burns's claimant pressed his case to rendition — no acceptance.
rationales.D: Background from the books: no state repealed the federal act — states could not repeal federal law; some passed personal liberty laws to hinder it instead.
rationales.general:
1. Line the four episodes up: Boston, Christiana, Syracuse, Boston again.
2. Sort them by ending: three freed by crowds, one returned by federal troops.
3. Name the pattern: Northern crowds fought the law in the streets, and the government sometimes fought back harder.
Remember: when the same law produces rescues and renditions side by side, the law is being contested, not obeyed.
